subject: desertOasisDiorama
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: desert oasis with palms, tents and camels.
Style: low-poly whimsical mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning a desert oasis diorama as a single module—palms, tents, and camels as scenery, with camels needing proper skeleton rigs. I'll use one root joint at the origin with camel joints parented beneath it, keeping the SDK API usage careful and the code reasonably compact but robust.

Working out the scale: a miniature diorama with base radius around 2 meters and camels about half a meter long. I'll attach all static props explicitly to the root joint using the bone option, since nearby camel joints could otherwise steal nearest-joint assignment, and I'm considering making palm trunks into chains for some added sway animation.

Designing the palm trees now: a four-joint trunk chain swept along its path, with a crown of fronds arranged in a ring at the top joint. Each frond is a bezier sweep with a flattened box cross-section that tapers to a point, curving upward then drooping at the tip, all bound to the top joint's bone.

Fronds should droop toward the tips, so I'll add an up vector to lean the sweep upward. For each frond direction I'm computing a cubic bezier with four explicit points (base, two control points curving outward and up, then dipping at the tip) rather than relying on a ring, attaching it to the top joint bone directly. Now I'm sizing the palm overall, roughly 0.9m tall with a base radius of 2.

Scaling the whole scene for whimsy: palm ~1.0 tall with 0.5-long fronds, tents ~0.7 wide, camels ~0.6 long and 0.55 tall, accepting the proportions are stylized rather than realistic. I'm laying out the oasis scene with a base radius of 2.2, placing the pond off-center as an irregular ellipse around (0.2, 0, 0.3), and planning the sand base to sit slightly above the water level.

I'm figuring out the pond as a flattened ellipse disc just above the sand, giving it a mottled teal color and surrounding it with a grass ring and stones, then designing the base as a layered lathe shape with a darker clay stratum beneath the sand layer.

For coloring I'll use a mottle paint for the sandy top layer and stripes paint along the y-axis for the clay strata beneath it. Then I'm adding dunes using flattened, partially buried spheres sunk into the sand surface.

I need to keep dunes within the base radius so they don't hang over the edge awkwardly, scaling and rotating them for natural placement. I'm defining the ground top height around y=0.27 and working out the lathe profile points so the surface slopes realistically from edge to center.

Now I'm planning the palm trees: five arranged around the pond, each built as a chain of four joints following a curved catmull-rom trunk path, with sequential joint and chain naming per palm.

For the trunk I'll sweep along the chain with a tapering radius and add ring-like bands using stripes along the y-axis for visual texture, keeping a low-poly look with 7-sided sections. Then I'll add a coconut cluster of small spheres beneath the crown joint.

Now I'm working out the fronds: eight of them with alternating droop, colored in two shades of green based on frond index for variation, plus small yellow-orange spheres for dates. Writing the frond width function...

I'm deciding to keep the sweep-based frond shape rather than a flat extruded leaf outline, since curved fronds riding along a single bone joint are simpler that way—skipping the serrated edge detail for now and considering using two sweeps per frond instead.

For the scene's tents, I'm planning a mix: one striped conical pavilion tent built as a lathed octagon with angled stripe paint, plus a ridge tent extruded from a triangular profile along the z-axis, centered on its thickness, with an overhanging fabric canopy slab near the front entrance.

I'll add a small extruded dark triangle as a door, slightly offset in front of the ridge tent, and work out custom paint logic using the x-coordinate to create vertical gable stripes rather than relying on a built-in stripe function.

For the lathe cone tent, I'm figuring out angular stripes by dividing the angle into 30-degree wedges (normalized to avoid negative values) to get 12 alternating segments. I'm also planning to restructure the ridge tent's roof as two slanted slabs instead of a prism, add protruding tent poles with finials at the ridge ends, and include guy ropes running from the eaves to small ground pegs. Then I start setting up the round pavilion tent using a lathe profile.

Working out the roof outline coordinates...

Working out the 12-gon wall geometry, door placement and thickness around z=0.49, plus finial details—a gold sphere, pennant flag, and pole rod at the apex.

Now I'm sketching the camel as the key creature: a dromedary with one hump, roughly 0.62m at hump height and 0.33m legs, built from a spine/neck/head/jaw/tail chain plus four IK legs. I'm setting up a local coordinate system facing +Z with a transform helper that applies yaw rotation and origin offset to every point and direction, so each camel instance can be placed and rotated consistently.

Mapping out the camel's proportions now—body barrel height, hump position, neck curve from shoulder up through to the head, and skull orientation with snout length, before moving into leg placement.

Working out leg geometry next: fore and hind limbs with knee/hock bends in opposite directions, structured as two-segment chains ending in a foot pad.

For two camels I need unique joint names, so I'll just suffix the second one's names with "_a"/"_b" like "hipFL_a" to keep things simple while still readable. Then for the body I'm planning to loft the spine as a chain of stations from rump to chest with varying width and height along a bone curve.

For the skeleton hierarchy, I'll explicitly assign every joint's parent rather than relying on nearest-joint defaults—starting with a camel root/pelvis joint, then building the spine chain forward from there.

Branching from spine: neck leads to head and jaw, tail extends backward from the hips, hind legs attach to the hips, and front legs attach to the last spine joint at the chest. I'll have the body geometry sweep along the spine chain as the core shape.

Actually a simpler approach: I can extend the spine path backward using a sweep extend parameter to create a rounded rump cap, then define the spine chain with just three catmull points for hips, mid, and chest, naming two joints to match the spans.

For the chest tip joint, which becomes the parent for the neck and front legs, I'll size the barrel radius so it's slightly narrower at the hips and widest in the middle, shifting the profile slightly downward to suggest a hanging belly.

For the hump, I'm attaching a flattened sphere near the top of the body, positioned along the first spine joint and scaled slightly taller than wide to give it that camel-hump silhouette. Now I'm thinking through adding a saddle blanket by looping a band around the body at one of the spine joints, cutting through the surface at that cross-section.

For the band geometry, I need to sweep along a closed loop path around the body with a section width oriented along the binormal direction, so it wraps like a flat strip rather than a tube.

I'll add a slight lift to avoid z-fighting with the body surface, and apply this blanket stripe treatment for both camels with distinct colors. The loop should be safe since the cutting plane clearly intersects the body mesh at that height, and loop picks the nearest valid ring around the given point.

For camel B specifically, I want to add a cargo pack: two flattened-sphere sacks positioned on either side of the spine, tied with a rope detail, plus a saddle blanket draped over the hump area for camel A.

Now I'm building the neck as a three-segment catmull-rom chain rising forward from the chest toward the head base, with the sweep radius narrowing from thick at the chest to slender near the head, rounded caps at both ends, parented to the chest/spine joint.

For the head, I'm placing the head joint at the neck's end point, aiming it forward-and-down toward the snout, and working out how to express local-space coordinates (forward/up/left-right) for positioning features like the eyes symmetrically using the model's local axes rather than world axes.

I realize it's simpler and more reliable to compute eyes, ears, and nostrils as explicit world-space points derived from the head's base position plus offset vectors in camel-space, and bind them directly to the head bone rather than relying on the local-coordinate helper, since the head joint's own rotation doesn't need to factor into placement.

Now I'm laying out the head geometry in camel-local coordinates — placing the skull capsule, muzzle, and jaw as a sequence of tapered segments running from the base of the skull down to the drooping lips, defining the snout's long dromedary shape.

Adding eyes with tiny highlights and whimsical long eyelashes, small cones for ears and forelock tufts, plus cheek fluff and a chin beard. Now I'm figuring out neck mane tufts along the underside using a sweep-based placement helper to scatter shaggy hair spikes along the neck tube.

I'll countershade the body paint with a mottled tan blending into a lighter belly, sharing that paint variable across body, legs, neck, hump, and head so patterns flow continuously. For legs I'm sweeping tube geometry along each joint chain with tapering radii, adding knee knobs and small sphere foot pads.

Now I'm checking foot placement so the flattened pad spheres and tapered leg sweep ends sit just above ground level, nudging the y-offsets by a few millimeters to avoid clipping below the sand plane while staying within tolerance of the model's overall height.

Now I'm working out the camel's hip and shoulder joint positions relative to the sand height, placing hind hips under the hips joint and front hips under the chest joint so each leg chain attaches correctly, then setting up the limb bend directions for the front legs' knee articulation.

For whimsy I'll make the camel chunkier with bigger pads and knee calluses. For the tail, I'm building a small chain from the hips using a curved path with tapering sweep radius and a tuft at the end, figuring out where the rump actually sits once the body's cap extension is accounted for so the tail root lines up correctly.

Checking overall proportions now: body spans from the tail end around z=-0.385 to the chest around z=0.375, giving roughly 0.76 length, with height to the hump near 0.62 and to the head near 0.88, which feels reasonably close to a real camel's scale relative to the tents and palms in the scene.

For variety I'll add three camels: a large saddled one standing near the tent at a slight yaw, a second one carrying cargo, and a smaller calf at 0.55 scale for a whimsical touch, reusing a shared camel-building function with scale and id parameters. I'm checking that the polygon budget stays reasonable -- each camel built from sweeps should only need a few thousand triangles, well within the 60k limit, and the part count per camel (body, hump, neck, head, eyes, etc.) stays manageable.

Now I'm tallying total parts across camels, palms, tents, and scenery to stay under a thousand, and counting joints per camel (hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, tail, legs) to keep the full skeleton budget under 160 joints, trimming the palm chains to three joints each to help stay within range. I'm also noting the color limit of 64 flat colors doesn't include paint layers.

For the pond, I'm building layered cylinders for the grass ring and wet sand rim, scaling radii and heights so the grass ring sits slightly above the sand ring, both ellipse-shaped around the water.

Adding ripple torus rings for the water surface, scaled to lie flat and elliptical, positioned just above the water top. For grass, I'm planning clusters of small cones around the pond edge, keeping part counts reasonable by merging geometries per color rather than instancing dozens of individual meshes.

I'm also adding a small arm cactus with capsule shapes and a pink flower, a campfire with log and flame cones ringed by stones, and oasis details like a lathe-turned water jar, striped carpets, cushions, and bunting strung between the tent and palm using triangles swept along a curved path.

I'll orient the rope sweep along x since the palm and tent are placed roughly along that axis, using a catmull path with sag for the sweep radius and explicit bone roots for unbound points. Every camel part needs an explicit bone reference since only sweep chains get automatic bone assignment, and I'm considering adding a small sun disc to the diorama for the sky.

Skipping the floating cloud idea since nothing should hang above the scene, but I'll add a small stepped pyramid at the back-left rim using a low-segment cone lathe for a desert touch, plus distant dunes. Now I'm setting up the code imports and helper functions to start building the scene.

Confirming mottle is exported, then I'm setting up the build function with a metadata export and starting the base joint hierarchy for the oasis diorama, defining the root joint position and base vector helper.

I'm lathing the base rock formation with a cross-section profile, then coloring it using a paint function that assigns strata bands by height—darker clay tones near the bottom transitioning to lighter layers higher up.

For the top, I'm adding a second lathe for the sandy cap, sharing the rim radius with the base, and mottling it with alternating sand tones for a textured, weathered look.

I'm thinking the base might read better as a low-poly 14-gon, and I'm mapping out where the sand surface sits relative to edge slopes, keeping dunes and camel figures within a safe inner radius so nothing clips the sloped rim. For dunes, I'm scattering flattened, scaled spheres partially buried into the sand to suggest mounds, positioning them asymmetrically around the center while staying inside the usable radius.

Let me pin down the dune positions and sizes so none exceed the 1.95 radius limit, adjusting dune B's center inward to keep it safely within bounds, and checking the others fit too.

For the ripple texture on the dunes, I'll add subtle stripe shading between light and dark sand tones along a slightly tilted axis with gentle wobble, keeping it understated since parameter semantics aren't fully certain.

For the pyramid, I'm setting up a lathe shape with 4 segments using a simple triangular profile.

Now I'm laying out the scene geometry: placing the pond center, then positioning several palm trees around it with leaning variations, and planning where the tents will sit relative to the pond and palms.

Round pavilion tent T1 goes near (-1.05, -0.35) with its door facing roughly forward, kept simple with front-facing orientation rather than complex rotation. Ridge tent T2 is placed further back at (-0.1, -1.0), elongated along the x-axis with its door also facing front.

For T2, I'm thinking of it as a triangular-prism silhouette extruded along x, with the ridge running along z so the gable faces the camera — width 0.6, depth 0.8, door centered at z=+0.4, plus a small front canopy with two poles. I keep refining camel B and its nearby calf's positions and yaw angles, then work through camel A's placement near the pond edge, checking its body length against the pond radius so its legs don't awkwardly overhang the slope boundary.

Let me shrink the pond slightly to a smaller oval and reposition camel A so it spans grass comfortably with its head extending just to the water's edge for a natural drinking pose. Then I start placing the palm trees around the pond — one leaning near the left edge, another tall one further out, and work toward positioning a tent in the background.

Checking P2 and P3 against the pond and grass edges, both sit acceptably at the boundary. I'm placing a camel with its head dipping toward the pond near the grass edge, and sketching out a campfire position in front of tent T1, adjusting coordinates so it doesn't overlap the palm cluster.

Then I work through the carpet placement in front of T1's door, sizing it to sit just outside the doorway without colliding with the fire, and checking distances between the fire and a second camel (B) angled at 60 degrees to confirm no overlap.

I'm also checking water jars next to T2's tent and palm P3's trunk placement, finding they collide with T2's front gable, so I shift T2's position leftward and recheck its distance to T1.

But I'm worried the rope might clip through the sloping tent roof since the roof's slope is steep — comparing the drop-over-radius ratio to figure out if the rope clears it as it exits toward the palm.

Now I'm sketching out the palm-tree generator: computing a base point, then three control points that curve toward a lean direction and height using interpolation weights, building a catmull-rom spline through them, and chaining joints along that spine for the trunk's bone structure. I'm working through naming conventions for the joints so each palm instance gets a unique prefix.

Sweeping the trunk geometry along the spline with a tapering radius function, adding a banded paint pattern based on vertical position to simulate trunk rings, and flaring the base radius with an exponential falloff for a natural root shape...

Now I'm attaching a crown joint at the treetop, then distributing nine fronds radially around it, each with randomized length and an arching curve defined by multiple control points sweeping outward and upward from the crown...

Box sections taper nicely with point caps at the tips. I'm adding layered fronds, a few young upright shoots at the crown center, and clusters of date spheres and coconuts beneath the foliage, then moving to code the palm tree function itself.

Writing camel helper function...

Defining more joints...

Building the body sweep...

Now I'm continuing the facial geometry: a tapered muzzle capsule, a small nose pad sphere colored darker than the coat, tiny dark nostril spheres, and starting the lower jaw capsule.

Adding a lower lip bump at the chin and checking that the jaw and muzzle capsules overlap enough to read as a closed mouth. Then moving on to the eyes, placing dark spheres with small white highlight dots symmetrically on each side.

For the sleepy eyelid effect, I'm adding a small coat-colored sphere positioned slightly above and covering the upper half of the white eye sphere, giving it a half-closed look. For ears, I'm placing small cones angled outward and back from the head using the part helper with a normalized direction vector.

Adding more fur details...

Still defining leg limb geometry...

Placing the sacks at offset positions along the body with a tan color and dark strap details, maybe small cones for ties. Adding roof paint and eave trim...
